extracted.intended_audience: poets/playwrights, dramatists, and students of poetics/literary theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing and evaluating classical tragedy: what plots, incidents, characters, and verbal performance make a successful tragic play (Aristotelian poetics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation should be of actions (not mere events)
rubrics_metrics.description: "poeta: imitetur autem nihil aliud, quam actiones ipsas" — the poet must imitate actions themselves, not merely unrelated happenings or ornamentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The work should present whole actions (praxis) rather than disconnected incidents; imitation of true events is permitted only insofar as they are the sort of events that could plausibly be actions in a plot. Avoid treating isolated occurrences as if they were a coherent action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid episodic, unconnected plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodic (episdodicae) stories—episodes imported from elsewhere that do not follow or connect—are the worst kind of fable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not stitch together loosely related episodes (ornaments 'advecta') with no necessary nexus; such 'episodic' composition results from ignorance or pandering to actors. The plot must have internal causal connexion so episodes follow from one another plausibly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy should imitate a complete (perfect) action
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitatio tragica non solum est perfecta actionis sed etiam terribilium et miserabilium — tragedy ought to imitate a whole/complete action, typically dreadful and pitiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a complex, unified action (with beginning, middle, end) rather than fragmentary or open-ended sequences. The best tragic actions produce pity and fear by showing a coherent causal progression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia (reversal) must be causally grounded and admirable
rubrics_metrics.description: Peripetia = admirabilis ac subita mutatio (a sudden reversal) which happens because of antecedent facts; it should arise from the constitution of the plot, not by chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversals should occur because of prior events either by necessary link or by verisimilitude; they should increase admiration because they seem to have arisen from causes rather than from mere fortune or accident (examples: Oedipus receiving news that produces the opposite result intended).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agnitio / recognition must arise from the plot's facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Agnitio = change from ignorance to knowledge; recognitions should be produced from the plot's antecedent facts, not fortuitously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best recognitions occur simultaneously with peripeteia; types are many (signs, innate marks, author-made clues, memory, syllogism, composite). Favor recognitions that grow naturally out of events rather than artificial contrivances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer peripeteia and anagnorisis linked (complex plot)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex (implexa) plots are those whose chief power lies in peripeteia and agnitio; the best tragedies are 'implexae' with reversal and recognition interconnected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the plot so that reversal and recognition occur from the same plot mechanics (often simultaneously), producing the strongest emotional effect (pity/fear).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathos (perpessio) — include fitting sufferings to arouse pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Perpessio = action bringing suffering, severe pains, deaths, tortures; these are legitimate means to create pity and fear in tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sufferings may be shown by apparatus (spectacle) or by the action itself, but the best effect is produced when the listener, even without spectacle, feels horror and pity from the narrated events. Avoid gratuitous monstrous spectacle that lacks artistic integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts of tragedy and their proper placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy's parts by quantity and place: prologus, episodium (episode), exodus, choric parts (parodus, stasimon). These are the common components of all tragedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the prologue before the chorus entrance (parodus); episodes are placed between full choric songs; exodus concludes the play without further choral song. Know the function of parodos (first choral entrance) and stasimon (stationary chorus song).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prologue as integral opening
rubrics_metrics.description: Prologus is an integral part of tragedy placed before the parodus to open the plot (e.g., Creon in Oedipus announces the circumstances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the prologue to establish necessary background before the chorus and episodes begin; it should belong to the action and not be extraneous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus must function as part of the whole action
rubrics_metrics.description: The chorus represents a group but in practice is treated as one interlocutor; choric songs are not independent fables but parts of the tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chorus should contribute to the unity of the action and be appropriate in what it sings; do not let the chorus behave as an unrelated narrative element or overshadow the plot's coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters should be morally good or at least not depraved
rubrics_metrics.description: One important trait: characters ought to be BONI, i.e., morally good or of noble quality rather than wicked (improbable and not fitting for tragic pity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make the tragic fall result from hardened wickedness; misfortune is more tragic when inflicted on persons with some virtue or excellence (a better-than-average person).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters must be congruent/appropriate to their roles
rubrics_metrics.description: CONGRUENTES: characters must behave appropriately for their sex, fortune, and role (e.g., men act manfully, women act as women should in the dramatic context).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mismatched behavior (e.g., a woman displaying masculine actions without cause). Maintain plausibility of character conduct in relation to social expectations and the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters should be similar to people of the current age (per quam similes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters ought to be similar to those now; they should resemble people of the present in their traits and speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is distinct from being 'good' — a character can be good and yet must be recognizable as a kind of person contemporary audiences accept as plausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters must be consistent (aequabiles)
rubrics_metrics.description: AEQUABILES: in all actions a character should show an evenness so that they are recognizably the same person across acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the character is changeable by plot necessity, maintain internal consistency (not jarring sudden transformations without cause). Avoid inaequabilitas that undermines imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic fall should stem from error (hamartia), not vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer that reversal to adversity originates from an error or great mistake rather than from gross wickedness; error produces pity/fear more aptly than wickedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not turn a good man into a villain by arbitrary conduct; a noble person who falls through ignorance or error is more tragic and fitting. Conversely, making wickedness the cause disconnects from what is fitting for tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not alter traditional well-known outcomes unjustifiably
rubrics_metrics.description: Established tales whose chief outcome contains peripeteiae and suffering (e.g., Clytemnestra murdered by Orestes) should not be dissolved (i.e., change their principal result) unless the poet invents new but similar events or uses the old well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may invent similar plots or improve traditional tales but avoid arbitrary reversals of established climaxes that would reduce tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition techniques and ranking of effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Kinds of agnitio: by signs (natural or accidental), by poet's contrivance (artificial signs), by memory, by syllogism (reasoning), composite (paralogism), and best of all: recognitions that emerge gradually from the events themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer recognitions that unfold from the story's facts (most effective); avoid clumsy artifices like improbable signs or overly contrived authorial devices except where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering and exposition: general exposition first, then insert episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: Put the general exposition before the action; after names and the general setup, insert episodes appropriate to their places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish situation and characters clearly (universal exposition) before episodes. Ensure episodes are accommodated to the main plot and do not interrupt logical sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the 'nexus' (conjunction) and 'solution' (denouement) properly
rubrics_metrics.description: Nexus = the chain drawn from the beginning to the point of change; Solutio = that which extends from the point of change to the end. Both are essential parts of the plot structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between events that occurred offstage (often nexus) and those onstage (solution). Both nexus and solution require careful craftsmanship; avoid sloppy dissolution of the plot after an expertly constructed nexus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genres/species of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedies are of four kinds: IMPLEXA (complex, with peripeteia and recognition), PATHETICA (emphasizing bitter sufferings), MORALIS (expressing noble morals), and SIMPLEX (simple, without reversal/recognition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for excellence within whatever species you choose; the complex (implexa) that combines reversal and recognition often yields the highest effect, but pathetic and moral types have their own merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making an epic out of a tragedy (length and multiplicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not turn a tragedy into an epic by making it a concatenation of many actions or by making each part an independent long episode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy should be composed within tighter bounds than epic; avoid long sprawling plots that lose unity. Large numbers of disparate incidents risk destroying tragic dignity and coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle (apparatus) is inferior to plot but may aid terror
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle and stage apparatus can make things appear terrible, but the poet of superior skill composes so that the tale itself, even without spectacle, evokes horror and pity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely primarily on the artistic construction of plot and character; spectacle should not substitute for proper plot devices. Monstrous spectacle (e.g., mere stage tricks) has little commonality with true tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extraneous machinery for events that should be intrinsic
rubrics_metrics.description: Machina (deus ex machina) may be used for matters outside the dramatic action; do not use machines to produce outcomes that ought to arise from the plot itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If something is part of the action-day it should be represented by the action, not by mechanical intervention. Use machina only to handle matters external to the drama's imitated day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style/diction (elocutio) and sententiae should serve the play's effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Elocutionary ornaments and sententiae (brief moral or rhetorical sayings) belong to rhetoric but are used by the poet to clarify, move emotions (pity, fear, anger), amplify or diminish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose sententiae that fit the situation and help evoke the required emotions; rhetorical figures of pronunciation and delivery (mandatio, narratio, interrogatio, etc.) belong to actoric craft and influence effect, though they are technically separate from poetic theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronunciation and actoric figures are important technical parts of performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronouncing figures (mandatio, precatio, narratio, comminatio, interrogatio, responsio) and other vocal/physical techniques are part of the histrionic art and affect the reception of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While composing, be mindful of how lines will be delivered: syllable length, accent, timbre, and articulation influence intelligibility and emotional force. These technical performance aspects should be considered though they are distinct arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of signs (physical marks) for recognition is possible but less artful
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs (innate or accidental) like scars, tokens, or birthmarks can produce recognition but are less artful than recognition emerging from the series of events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using physical tokens, prefer those that plausibly yield recognition; beware of contrived or overly obvious tokens that reduce artistic subtlety. The poet's invented signs (auctoris factae) are acceptable but should not be the principal source of agnitio.
